title: Suspected acute hepatic porphyria (AIP)
consultQuestion: Weakness or neuropathy with severe abdominal pain, hyponatremia, or seizures — could this be an acute porphyric attack?
keyHistory: Recurrent severe abdominal pain without a clear cause after initial workup, especially in women 15–50 (AGA BPA 1)
Triggers: CYP450-inducing / porphyrinogenic drugs, progesterone (luteal phase), alcohol, tobacco, fasting, acute illness or stress (AGA BPA 6)
Prior similar attacks — mean delay to diagnosis ~15 years (AGA)
Family history — autosomal dominant with low penetrance (AGA BPA 3)
keyExam: Severe abdominal pain without peritoneal signs; cross-sectional imaging unrevealing (AGA)
redFlags: Seizures — barbiturates, hydantoins, carbamazepine, and valproate are contraindicated (AGA BPA 5)
Progressive weakness — porphyria is a listed GBS mimic (Leonhard 2019 Box 2)

differential.dx: Acute hepatic porphyria (AIP, HCP, VP; ALAD rare)
clues: Random urine ALA and PBG ≥5× ULN (creatinine-normalized) during an attack (AGA Table 2)
Progressive symmetric weakness with areflexia; CSF protein normal in 30–50% in week 1 (Leonhard 2019)
Mild urine porphyrin elevation only — not diagnostic of AHP and a common cause of overdiagnosis (AGA BPA 2)

workup.test: Random (spot) urine ALA, PBG, and creatinine
notes: Collect BEFORE hemin — hemin normalizes ALA/PBG (AGA BPA 4)
Diagnostic: ALA and PBG ≥5× ULN normalized to creatinine; 24-h urine not recommended (AGA BPA 2, Table 2)
Reference-lab send-out; results often take 1–2 weeks; a rapid PBG test is FDA-approved but rarely stocked (AGA)
Monitor during the attack; correct hyponatremia slowly (AGA BPA 5)
Confirms AHP type; not for initial screening (AGA BPA 3)

decisionRules.condition: Woman 15–50 with unexplained recurrent severe abdominal pain after initial workup
decisionRules.recommendation: Screen for AHP with random urine ALA, PBG, creatinine
evidenceNote: AGA 2023 BPA 1–2 (expert review; statements carry no formal evidence rating)

decisionRules.recommendation: Presume AHP and treat; confirm type later with genetic testing

decisionRules.condition: Attack severe enough to need admission
decisionRules.recommendation: IV hemin daily, preferably into a high-flow central vein
Avoid barbiturates, hydantoins (phenytoin/fosphenytoin), carbamazepine, valproate; magnesium, benzodiazepines, and levetiracetam appear safe

initialSteps: Stop CYP450-inducing / porphyrinogenic drugs; check every drug in an AHP drug-safety database (porphyria.org; drugs-porphyria.org) (AGA BPA 5–6)
IV hemin 3–4 mg/kg once daily, typically 4 days (3–5 days), via PICC or central port, after the urine sample is sent (AGA BPA 4)
IV carbohydrate ~300 g/day early in the attack; treat pain and nausea aggressively (AGA BPA 5)
disposition: Admit if the attack needs IV hemin (AGA BPA 4)
≥4 attacks/year: outpatient prophylaxis (hemin or givosiran) with a porphyria specialist (AGA BPA 7)
institutionVaries: Urine ALA/PBG sample handling (light protection, refrigeration/freezing) — follow the reference lab's instructions
Reference lab and turnaround for ALA/PBG
pearls: Don't screen with urine porphyrins alone — ALA and PBG are porphyrin precursors and are not included in porphyrin tests (AGA BPA 2)
Between attacks, 15–44% with sporadic AIP have normal urine ALA/PBG; in AIP they can stay elevated for months after an attack, in HCP/VP they fall quickly (AGA)
Porphyria is in the motor-CIDP differential (EAN/PNS 2021 Table 4)
sources: Wang B, et al. AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review. Gastroenterology 2023;164:484-491. doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2022.11.034
Leonhard SE, et al. Diagnosis and management of Guillain-Barré syndrome in ten steps. Nat Rev Neurol 2019;15:671-683. doi:10.1038/s41582-019-0250-9
